_description:
# Daemon procs: direct control, bypassing the kernel

Use aos-daemon-ctl for arbitrary procs on one daemon; a sent letter is not proof that the requested change finished. To go through the kernel, use `aos-agent ctl` (`aos/cli/agent.json`).
add:
# add: attach a proc

```sh
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d add --name tick tick.json      # a loop config: runs again and again
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d add --name job job.sh -- 3     # runs once; ARGS after --
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d where --stack tick             # /srv/d/procs/tick
```

add prints a letter name. It detects a loop config (an object with `exec` and no `argv`) by its structure; other targets run once as exec procs, and only those take ARGS after `--`. A definition folder runs its `_entry`; to attach an agent use `aos-agent ctl add`. Exit 0 of a run-once proc removes its row; a known nonzero exit stays `stopped` with a reason (`failed to start: exited within 3s of wake/start (code 3)`). `--auto-restart` restarts it whenever it exits. `--ws`, `--stack`, `--ws-json`, `--stack-json`, `--path-json`, `--limits` work as for `aos-agent ctl add`. where on a name not on the table = `ProcMissing`.
lifecycle:
# stop, sleep, pause, rm

All procs can stop, start, sleep and wake regardless of launch syntax. stop writes the proc's public ctl window and waits for exit (no SIGTERM fallback): row `stopped`, back with `start`. sleep sends SIGTERM (SIGKILL after 10 s): row `sleeping`, back with `wake`. Wrong pairs give `PhaseBad`. pause/resume write `{"cmd": "pause", "seq": N}` to the ctl window, print N and wait up to `--timeout-s` (default 5) for it to apply; a timeout warns and exits 0; the program decides whether to read it. rm detaches; the stack stays, and it does not ask. The ctl filename comes from a nonempty `ctl` in the parent-written loop config, otherwise ctl.json. Sleeping rows wake at the next daemon start.
letters:
# Letters, waiting and the kernel

add/rm/stop/start/sleep/wake print a letter name and wait up to `--timeout-s` (default 3) for the daemon to claim it. A still-queued letter gives a warning and exit 0. After the claim it briefly reads the daemon's reply: a refused letter (bad body) is an error `BodyBad` with the reason. Otherwise claim does not prove application: check with `ls`. `--reply-to BOX` sends only; read the reply yourself (`applied: true|false`). It excludes `--timeout-s`.

aos-daemon-ctl is the tool for naming one daemon: it always sends straight to that daemon's ctl mailbox, never reads `$AOS_KERNEL`, and bypasses any kernel; it works where Linux permissions let you write that mailbox. `aos-agent ctl` routes via `$AOS_KERNEL` and warns `routing via AOS_KERNEL=PATH`. A sleeping or stopped kernel is the system designer's risk: wake it by hand with `aos-daemon-ctl wake NAME` (stopped: `start`).
ls:
# ls, ping, poke

```sh
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d ls
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d ping        # replied in 108 ms
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d poke --all  # run a full round now
```

```text
_clock	running	1082359	-	-	-
# daemon: running (pid 1082357)
# root daemon (no supervisor)
```

ls columns (TAB): NAME PHASE PID CODE WS REASON. The last two lines start with `# `: whether this daemon runs, and what its supervisor thinks; skip them in parsers. `ls -j` prints one object. ls and where only read files: they do not prove liveness. ping waits for a reply (`DaemonFailed` on timeout). poke is a doorbell: `--ctl` (default), `--mail` or `--all`; write ctl or send a letter first.
shutdown:
# shutdown: stop the whole daemon

```sh
aos-daemon-ctl -d stacks/root shutdown
# daemon at /.../stacks/root stopped (ctl seq 1); 2 procs asleep, they wake when it starts again
```

Every running proc sleeps and stays on the table; starting the daemon again wakes them. It waits up to `--timeout-s` (default 15); still running = `StillRunning`: do not commit or copy the stacks yet, run shutdown again. A stop already in progress stays stopped, a sleep in progress becomes sleeping, an rm in progress is removed; if kill -9 interrupts shutdown, the next start reaches the same result.
prune:
# prune: check rows and remove old ones

```sh
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d prune
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d prune --older-than 7d
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d prune --older-than 7d --apply
```

`prune` prints each suspicious row as `NAME: PHASE: PROBLEM`: missing stacks, ctl files that are not JSON objects, stale process identities, and stopped reasons. Findings alone exit 0.

`--older-than` (a positive integer plus `s`, `m`, `h` or `d`) selects only stopped/sleeping rows whose latest stack change (the stack folder and its direct files) is older; rows without a stack are never selected. Preview lines are `NAME: would remove (last change ISO_TIME)`. `--apply` requires `--older-than`, uses the same letter path as `rm` and prints `NAME: removed`; all stack and workspace files stay.
sweep:
# sweep: one sweeper round now

```sh
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d sweep --dry-run
aos-daemon-ctl -d /srv/d sweep --purge --dry-run   # _clock: would purge 1 file(s) (3130 bytes) in ...
```

sweep runs the same code as the `_sweeper` row (`aos/cli/sweeper.json`) inside this command, so it works when that row is paused or missing. `--purge` deletes every stderr archive of this daemon (asks on a terminal; `-y` skips). Here archives are deleted by age only with `--retention-days N`. Another sweeper busy longer than `--timeout-s` (default 30) = `SweepBusy`. `-j` prints the round as JSON.
